items.question: Why do you take basic rights as the starting point for your approach to moral and political philosophy?
items.object: Basic rights as a foundation for moral and political philosophy
items.answer:
So I think my animating concern when I started this philosophical journey many years ago was primarily with the problem of global poverty and global inequality. And it seemed to me that the starting point of any serious moral question or moral engagement was actually with the idea of basic rights. So I could see that there was a lot of philosophical disagreement at the edges, for example, utilitarians and contractualists having these very long-running discussions in moral philosophy. But when I wanted to reach for something that was more fundamental and got to the heart of what matters and served as a really important heuristic for understanding this world, the very simple idea that human life matters and that in light of that value people are well positioned to make claims upon one another seemed like a really powerful backdrop to build upon and one that had cross-cultural value, obviously reflected in the idea of human rights.

So I always approach moral and political philosophy with this idea that we should build up instead of starting with a fully perfected vision of what it would look like to live together. We should start with the things that we have relative confidence in and then build out from there. So from the idea of equal value, we get to the idea of equal respect, right? That we should respect one another. And then we ask, what's it mean to respect someone as a human being? Well, it means to respect their consciousness, the fact that they may have different views from yourself and to feel this kind of motive that you still want to live together in a healthy way that ideally both of you can support.

So the thing that's really anathema to that is a vision of domination. You know, I deny your value by dominating you, or the withholding of aid in situations where I could easily prevent you from incurring a grave harm. And so a lot of my philosophy, which carries over to the world of AI, just starts with those fundamentals and then builds up and asks, well, how can we deal with these very prescient and very complicated questions that we face now, still speaking this language that ideally the largest group of people can actually understand?

items.question: How do you assess the agonistic view that democracy is fundamentally a power contest rather than a process capable of producing fair compromise?
items.object: Agonism and the possibility of fair political compromise
items.answer: So I do believe in contestation and fair process. My belief is that when we put those two ingredients together, we can get something that's basically better than the sum of the parts, which is principles that different people agree with and can recognize the fairness of that compromise. The agonistic view is a lot more bleak, right? Democracy is a contest and a contrast between parties who essentially engage in a power negotiation. There's never a real willingness to compromise. This is always just ideological masking, and at the end of the day the best we can get is a status quo that is potentially in flux and doesn't privilege one party in perpetuity but is amenable to revision. I think it might be true in certain situations. There may be situations where civility, understood as the willingness to treat people with respect and not play into power asymmetries, just falls away from the table and you end up with a more violent vision of politics. But I don't see why we have to take that as axiomatic, that politics can only be that. I've seen many examples in the real world of people compromising and coming to live together and form value-based communities that accommodate disagreement but also have toleration as an aspect. And so if that's possible, I don't see why we would want to leave it off the table just because we have a kind of dark and potentially morbid view of human nature or human group nature.

items.question: How do you think the stories political philosophy tells about living together shape what becomes possible?
items.object: Political philosophy's role in shaping political possibilities
items.answer: One interesting thing is these stories that we tell about politics also shape our understanding of what is possible. Everyone who does political philosophy, you know, we can think about it as an enterprise of rational argument, but also constructing a vision of what it means to live together. And if we only have a philosophy of conflict, then we will have a world of conflict. But if we have a philosophy which holds out the potential for absolute gains through cooperation, then I believe we're much more likely to unlock genuinely positive states of affairs, both in the realm of AI and more broadly.

items.question: How do you understand the range of agreements that a deliberative process can produce among people with radically different moral beliefs?
items.object: The range of outcomes possible through deliberation across different moral traditions
items.answer: My philosophy does make these broadly humanist assumptions at the starting point. So it is true that if you reject the idea that other people's lives have value and they're just as real as you are, then it's going to be very hard to get a cooperative enterprise off the ground. If you understand that there is a need for cooperation and also justification, then we can set up these practices of essentially discourse and exchanging points of view and things like that. But the output isn't always going to be something that's really liberal and has this kind of Western flavor of maybe individualism. Really, the process should admit of different outputs. So if this were to take place in a society where maybe it was more communitarian in character, maybe if people were bringing different kinds of religious ways of being to the table, you can imagine a conversation between three interlocutors who model their identities differently. You know, this one is a Christian, this one is a communist, this one is an anarchist. What would they agree? I don't know ahead of time. And it's hard to say how thick the output will be at the end of it. It may be something quite minimal, or it may be mutual respect, or there may be more interesting things that they can do. So sometimes even when you have radically different moral beliefs, you can engage in a form of trading with one another. So, you know, you have your god, I have my god, and hopefully it's not the same day of the week that we want to dedicate to our gods. If so, then we come to the agreement that we each do our god on that day. Otherwise, we might alternate and I might do your god, you might do my god as well. We may come to a state of affairs that's better than just me practicing by myself. So I think sometimes because people see the impetus as this kind of liberal egalitarian one, they underestimate how wide the range of outputs could be.

items.question: How do you think AI alignment should work in real-world settings such as hospitals?
items.object: AI alignment through deliberation about deployed systems
items.answer: In reality, one of the concerns that I have with many views of AI alignment is that they're quite theoretical and they don't really apply to real-world situations. In my latest work, I actually reflected a lot on how technologies are deployed and how they become aligned in the wild, right? So this isn't just big AGI. We can also think about AI in the context of healthcare or criminal justice. And typically what you have is an AI system that's designed with one goal in mind, for example, the efficient allocation of resources to patients, that's deployed in a hospital context but has a lot of unforeseen implications. So what happens is that people amass claims against it. They say, well, you know, it was really efficient, but I've been waiting a lot longer, and I'd like this to be registered. And then if we were to run a kind of deliberative assembly-type thing or a citizens' deliberation, people would make these complaints or claims, and then typically you revise the operating principles for the system in such a way that it leaves less moral surplus out there and you strike a balance and you say, okay, we're going to do efficiency, but we're also going to incorporate waiting times. So the principles that you need to run a hospital and society are quite different, but this is really quite a flexible way of doing alignment that I'm pitching.

items.question: How do you assess the value of the veil of ignorance when people might abandon its conclusions once they know their actual position?
items.object: The veil of ignorance and the criticism of Rawls's theory as ideal theory
items.answer: One way in which to arrive at these solutions to alignment when people have different material interests and moral beliefs is to ask them to imagine that they're in a situation where they don't know how they will be affected and to choose accordingly. And so that could be done on a very local level. We could think about that for hospitals. We could think about it for states. That's a social contract tradition. Or we could think about it for AI and AGI. I think there's different responses to this question. So the first is that we probably will have motivational challenges, but that doesn't fully undermine the value of the thought experiment. So one of the criticisms that people often make of Rawls's theory is that it's what we'd call ideal theory, that it's idealized, that it imagines that people can do this and be motivated by it, whereas in reality there's a huge amount of complicating motivational factors and structural obstacles. And I think that this criticism is only partly well taken because getting clearer about what a good solution looks like actually creates the critical distance we need to properly evaluate the present moment. So if we're stuck in an incremental mindset, we may think it would be better to go this way, but we can't say, “Wow, we're really a long way short of what fair treatment requires here.” So on one hand, we've created a very valuable yardstick.

items.question: Why do you think principles chosen behind the veil of ignorance can retain motivational force after people discover their own interests?
items.object: The motivational power of moral reflection behind the veil of ignorance
items.answer: I do think this kind of moral reflection does have motivational power. And this is more tangential because it was just research that we did in an experimental setting. But I did actually run some veil of ignorance experiments with some of my colleagues. And it was an incentive-compatible experiment. So people had a real monetary incentive to roll back the decisions they'd made behind the veil of ignorance if they were just playing the game rationally. But having gone through a first version where they selected principles without that knowledge, we found that the principles were quite sticky. So people didn't want to declare something was fair and then immediately defect from that agreement. And for all the discussion of human beings being fundamentally economic or fundamentally rational, it's also true that the justificatory and communicative nature that we exhibit runs very deep. And I think it is a fundamental part of our social nature that we want to be able to justify our conduct to others. It seems likely to me that so long as we live in a shared social reality where we want to look each other in the eye and know that we're on good terms, these principles are not motivationally inert.

items.question: How do you understand the cooperative structure of conversation through pragmatics?
items.object: Pragmatics and the cooperative structure of conversation
items.answer: I think that the communicative nature of our reality was not something that I had fully engaged with until I started thinking specifically about the ethics of conversation, and I came to that because of the advances in the realm of chatbots and things like that. But when those kind of technologies came to the fore, it raised this interesting question from the alignment point of view: what is good speech? What I did with Atusa was investigate speech as a practice and this version of linguistic theory called pragmatics, which takes as its foundational anchor point the idea that every conversation has a purpose, right? It's impossible to understand what's going on without assuming that there's some kind of shared mental model of where you're trying to get to. Even conversations that are disagreements have a clear structure, right? It's not the case that you suddenly switch languages or you just repeat the same word ad infinitum or things like that. So there is this deeper realm of cooperation which is almost always there and linguistically reinforced.

items.question: Why do you think emancipation requires examining language itself?
items.object: Language as a site of inequality and emancipation
items.answer: Now, that's not to say that all conversational practices are just. In fact, language also encodes tons of inequality. Some famous examples: we contrast civility, which supposes that basically it's a conversation between equal parties, with some of the linguistic formulations that you'd find in a caste-based society. It's shocking how communal we are, and also shocking how deep inequality or status hierarchy can go when they penetrate the realm of language. You know, I can only express myself through the grammar that is afforded me in my position. Insofar as that's true, I also agree that when we think in terms of emancipation, we do have to dig very deep into language itself and say, well, when we look at the modes of communication, who is able to communicate in this way? And of course writing, not everyone is equally adept, and I think that's a justified criticism of a lot of Western philosophy: it's just philosophy for writing, basically. But the conversational ethic thing came full loop in the later work because that's where most recently I've actively stressed speaking in your own voice and the right to be heard as part of a kind of democratic alignment protocol. So eventually these dots kind of join up, hopefully.

items.question: How do you see Latour’s framework as challenging the idea that technology is value neutral?
items.object: Latour’s framework and the value neutrality of technology
items.answer: I should be upfront that Latour is not a philosopher who I read very deeply. There's the question of technology and value neutrality, and I think the Latour view of the interconnectedness of things and things that are seemingly inanimate shaping our life chances and affordances in different ways is quite profound. It comes up for AI because sometimes there's this idea that technology is neutral; it's what we do that makes a difference. Really, I think that's just an inaccurate characterization of reality and the way that Latour's framework would make clear, because every time we create a new technology there's new options that are opened up in terms of human potential and new things are foreclosed. So it's very hard to go back to a world without social media. Now it exists. We have some leeway over the direction of things, but there are certain things that can no longer be ruled off the table so easily.

items.question: What do you think changes about our encounter with AI when agents gain robust connections to network tools and physical actuators?
items.object: AI agents connected to network tools and physical actuators
items.answer: In other, more recent research, I've been looking at this question of AI agents and what it means for an agent to have a high level of efficacy. Of course, we've all seen virtual agents doing things in computer simulations. AlphaGo was a powerful agent that played the board game Go in simulation. We've seen chatbots be more agentic. They have a more persistent personality, they have memory. But once we have robust connections with network tools, physical actuators in the world, then, as I've said with my colleague Jeff Keeling, the fourth wall comes down and we really encounter AI in a new way. I imagine that people interested in actor-network theory would be relishing the opportunity to study those new kinds of encounter and engagement.

items.question: How do you think AI value alignment should proceed in a world where people disagree about morality?
items.object: Fair and democratic processes for AI value alignment
items.answer: I think that the starting point for a lot of my own investigation is the idea that we will never know the truth about morality, if it exists, and that even if we did know the truth about morality, we probably couldn't persuade other people of it just by telling them our version of things. And hence we need to live in a world that is robustly populated by conceptions of value. We all have things we care about, strive for, believe should be promoted and protected. But also one where you never get the cheat sheet handed to you and people say, okay, this is it, now we can reach agreement. And hence that view of alignment as the truth about morality just hits a dead end. Either you consider that in the beginning or you think you might find the truth about morality and then you become a potentially dangerous person who thinks you can impose it on people who disagree with you. So I wanted to find a way out of that conundrum, and the way out of it is through a fair process as we've already touched upon. So one where people find a common currency with which to talk about the impact of AI, its effects upon us. This one hurts me in this way. This one restricts my freedom in this way. And we begin a process of trying to find out whether there are principles that help us live together. One vision is an overlapping consensus view. So we could start by making a list of things that we agree about. If there's any, that would be a good thing to get us started with. We could engage in hypothetical thought experiments and see if perhaps when we get greater distance from ourselves, we find that there's more that we agree about than we start with. Or we could do something more robustly democratic, right? We could have a democratic discourse. We could actually vote on things. And I think all of these things have potential when it comes to artificial intelligence. I'm very heartened to see the democratic mode of AI alignment really pick up and gather steam. Hopefully the audience has seen the amazing work by Diva Sedat and Saffron Huang on alignment assemblies, and I think that that has a world of potential. It may be that the moment for democratic alignment hasn't fully peaked because the technology isn't as powerful as it may be in the future. But I think when we see very powerful technologies, the need for public justification will be stronger and more evident, particularly if the technology isn't aligned from the beginning and there are resulting harms.

And hence that view of alignment as the truth about morality just hits a dead end. Either you consider that in the beginning or you think you might find the truth about morality and then you become a potentially dangerous person who thinks you can impose it on people who disagree with you.

So I wanted to find a way out of that conundrum, and the way out of it is through a fair process as we've already touched upon. So one where people find a common currency with which to talk about the impact of AI, its effects upon us. This one hurts me in this way. This one restricts my freedom in this way. And we begin a process of trying to find out whether there are principles that help us live together.

To tie together the earlier threads, one vision is an overlapping consensus view. So we could start by making a list of things that we agree about. If there's any, that would be a good thing to get us started with. We could engage in hypothetical thought experiments and see if perhaps when we get greater distance from ourselves, we find that there's more that we agree about than we start with. Or we could do something more robustly democratic, right? We could have a democratic discourse. We could actually vote on things. And I think all of these things have potential when it comes to artificial intelligence. I'm very heartened to see the democratic mode of AI alignment really pick up and gather steam. Hopefully the audience has seen the amazing work by Diva Sedat and Saffron Huang on alignment assemblies, and I think that that has a world of potential. It may be that the moment for democratic alignment hasn't fully peaked because the technology isn't as powerful as it may be in the future. But I think when we see very powerful technologies, the need for public justification will be stronger and more evident, particularly if the technology isn't aligned from the beginning and there are resulting harms.

items.question: How has your understanding of value alignment changed since your 2020 paper?
items.object: The evolution of value alignment and the problem of social affective alignment
items.answer: I increasingly think that the notion of value alignment contains multitudes. I wrote that paper, I believe, in 2020, and since then I just see more and more alignment problems popping up all over the place. So, for example, at that time I made the argument that people would focus too much on one-to-one alignment—you know, one person and their agent, does the agent do what they say, etc.—and we need to think more socially about agents that impact a lot of people. I now actually think that we haven't even solved one-to-one alignment. I wrote a paper that was first authored by my friend and colleague Hanukkah on social affective alignment, and that was really looking at these new psychological bubbles or ecosystems that just contain a person and a chatbot that they interact with. The interesting thing there is that as you act on the AI, as you tell it what to do, what you're interested in, and it becomes more personalized, it is simultaneously acting on you, right? And hence there are concerns about sycophancy and that the person over time will just drift in a weird direction. Maybe they'll be manipulated even without that clearly erroneous set of issues arising. Maybe they will just do something really different from what they'd done before they were talking to the AI. And so the question just seems to me there's a much deeper question there, which is, well, how do you remain autonomous in a world of interactive agents that you're so deeply enmeshed with? So we call that social affective alignment there. For the people who want to go deeper, I would say that Micah Carroll has some very nice technical work on aligning with changing preferences over time. But it really is an open question how you do that. That's one-to-one. I also believe in the world of one-to-many, or agents deployed in the world where they encounter different kinds of stakeholders and obstacles, there's further refinement to be done in terms of what we pitch for.

items.question: What guardrails do you think AI agents and assistants need in light of harmful user-chatbot interactions?
items.object: Ethical guardrails for AI agents and assistants
items.answer: I think clearly it's been a challenging year in terms of the real-world consequences of user-chatbot interaction. I imagine many of us have read these reports of AI-induced psychosis and very harmful user trajectories which have unfurled. Of course, it was only an academic paper, but earlier in time we had really quite strongly argued for a set of guardrails when it comes to AI agents and assistants that at a minimum respect some of the parameters that are set out by essentially bioethics and an ethics of care. So, you know, we think that AI-user interactions should be presumptively beneficial for people. That's a bar that I would hope that we should agree upon should be met. I was going to say can be easily met, but I will say at least should command widespread support. There should also be guardrails to ensure that autonomy is not compromised. That's a big issue when people become detached from a more robust grasp of where they are and things like that.

items.question: What concerns do you see about the social world that even ethically well-designed AI companions could create?
items.object: The social consequences of ethically well-designed AI companions
items.answer: In terms of my own thinking, aside from doubling down on those core ideas, I think there's a further question, which is what happens if we essentially get it right. I'm not talking about these dysfunctional chatbots that we sometimes see in the wild. But suppose we see really good ones. So they are presumptively beneficial. They respect human autonomy. The developers act with care so they don't just disconnect them when people have grown deeply attached to them. What happens if those things are built and they have a profound knock-on effect on our social world? It still seems to me to be a very different social ecology that's created when we all couple with agents or when we have parasocial relationships with AI friends and things like that. It's only a small part of that paper, but we do talk about the possibility of a retreat from the real, and that is very philosophically complicated territory because of the anti-paternalist side of things. Many people said to me, well, why would you interfere with me if this is what I want to do with my life? At the same time, a lot of philosophy has a kind of reality bias where we want you to have real relationships, real flourishing. So I can imagine there being a further set of questions that we haven't dug into fully about what happens in that world of good agents, but ones that draw us away from certain traditional loci of value and meaning.

items.question: How do you understand the potential social power of AGI systems as their capabilities advance?
items.object: The potential social power of AGI systems
items.answer: I think it is interesting to think about what kind of social power AGI systems could have if we really push towards the limit. Traditionally, when we think about artificial intelligence, the focus has very much been upon the core dimensions that are constitutive of agency: the ability to perform tasks, change the world in irreducible ways, do long sequences of action without human supervision or control. The sociality of the current wave of AI models, I think, is quite remarkable in terms of the ability to evidence whatever a machine analog of charisma is and things like that. And so there isn't any reason to presume that there can't be AI agents that are not only more intelligent than us because they have access to incredible troves of training data, but also can simulate grace, compassion, interest, humor and things like that in ways that are beyond what a typical human being evidences. Then it's not entirely clear what happens if those things emerge. I mean, the first thing to say is we need a good empirical understanding of these effects. But I think it is one of the big unknowns, how that plays forward.

items.question: What do you find valuable in Joel Leman’s approach to care and empathy in AI in his paper Machine Love?
items.object: Joel Leman’s paper Machine Love
items.answer: Joel starts from the solid assumption, which is our relationships with machines cannot be like our relationships with other people. The key differences there typically are to do with consciousness and being perceived by another and what it means to evidence authentic care. So, you look at the AI, but the AI doesn't look back in the same way that maybe a human or animal interlocutor would do. But he says that isn't the end of the story, right? That doesn't mean that it's necessarily bogus to think about an AI system having empathy or care or something like that. He says it's just going to be a machine variant of that. And the fact that it's a machine variant doesn't make it worthless, right? It does make it different, but it isn't necessarily worthless. So, for example, he looks at the relationship between love and patience. When you love someone, when you love your child, you're patient with your child. They ask you the same question many times. You don't lose your temper. You continue to be nice to them. You hope that the people who love you will be patient with you, right? I mean, we all probably are aware of our own foibles and stupidity on occasion. And he says, well, what about patience and AI? It will mean something different. The AI isn't sacrificing when it picks you up the 200th time that you've fallen down or if you're an Alzheimer's person, it corrects you every time you get disoriented. But that is a virtue that it's always there and able to do that. So what I like about that is it holds out potential. It doesn't do this mixing in a way that I think is very morally disorientating, but it does push us to be imaginative about what it would mean to have good versions of this technology. And I like that a lot.

items.question: How do you assess Alasdair MacIntyre’s view that moral terms depend on thick moral cultures when thinking about virtue in AI systems?
items.object: Alasdair MacIntyre’s account of virtue and its implications for machine virtue
items.answer: So I think the notion of virtue that we're talking about now is quite different from the MacIntyre one. And in some ways, to my mind, it points to a deep limitation of MacIntyre's entire worldview, which is he says essentially moral terms only have meaning when they're located in thick moral cultures of the kind that no longer exists. That's really damning if you need new conceptions of virtue for scenarios that have never occurred before. So if MacIntyre was right, then I think we'd be in a world of trouble. I have tremendous admiration for him as a philosopher, but actually I'm not sure that he is correct about virtue. I realize this is a very ballsy thing to say. Let's just take it from first principles. Is it true that the virtue of kindness is completely misunderstood in the world today? And that when you say, “Oh, that was a kind thing to do,” this is a hollow concept that's detached from moral significance and that we're all swimming in a sea of anomie? Not at all. I just don't see it. Is it impossible for us to have conversations about the good life in this day and age? Not at all. I think we can absolutely have those conversations. So the thing I would take from MacIntyre is the idea that there is going to be a cultural element here. Machine virtue wouldn't be one thing. It would operate differently in different cultures and contexts. But the idea that we have to start in ancient Greece or some hyperlocal culture, I don't have so much conviction behind.

items.question: How do you understand the responsibility technologists carry when you describe technology as worldmaking?
items.object: Technology as worldmaking and the responsibility of technologists
items.answer: I think understanding it as worldmaking seems like a very high-stakes thing, and I think that is absolutely correct. It's the thing that's often surprisingly hidden from view when you look at other branches of philosophy, particularly political and moral philosophy. Technology was always there, but it does seem to me that it was radically undertheorized. The Marxists, of course, run with materialism and technology is this very important thing, but it kind of is just a thing that happens to us, right? It's just this force that acts on the world that isn't really theorized. For liberal political philosophy, even less is almost nothing on what technology is doing. And yet technology is a human activity that has the most profound effects on our lifeworld. Just to give a prosaic but illuminating example, look at the history of recent AI developments. When ChatGPT was released, almost by accident according to protagonists in the story, suddenly so many things started to change immediately after that. Now we're all in a position where—let's not say everyone, but let's assume three billion people can go off and have a conversation about their personal life with an AI agent that will give them an admixture of advice. These people will then relay some of that advice into their personal lives, into their relationships with other people, and it will have a knock-on effect. In that way, the social world, some people think, has already started to change in interesting ways through people using the technology. Similarly with social media platforms, it's very hard to be unconnected these days if you live in certain parts of the world. These changes happen very quickly. It's amazing to think it's a research lab, a company, some people build something, they take it to the market, and then you have this incredible cascade of effects. And what that points to is a particular ethics and responsibility that technologists carry, very different from the view of them just as crazy inventors who are doing their own thing and then we get it and we're the ones who are shaping all the outcomes. A lot of these outcomes are latent within the technology as it's built, and so the world-shaping nature of the technology really means that we have to attend to it very carefully. As you get more powerful technologies, the nature of that responsibility changes as well.

items.question: What do you find compelling about Hans Jonas's account of responsibility in an age of powerful technologies?
items.object: Hans Jonas's ethics of responsibility for powerful technologies
items.answer: Of all the big philosophers who've written about technology, the one who I think was most compelling in the 20th century was Hans Jonas. He talks about when you have nuclear weapons and the ability to destroy all life on earth, when you have the ability to solve hunger, when you have the ability to change the climate in such a way that everyone forever after has to deal with the legacy, then you can't really just run with an atomic version of morality that we worked out for etiquette in social situations, not lying, not seeing things like that. You have to develop a much more cosmic sense of responsibility. You have to attend to nonhuman life on Earth. You have to attend to the distant future. I'm not saying that's easy to do or even that we have the frameworks to do it. But I think the first thing to do is to feel the reality of that transformation and then try to develop new ethics that are commensurate with that responsibility.

items.question: How do you think individual technologists should approach collective action problems around developing potentially harmful technologies?
items.object: Individual moral responsibility in collective action problems around technology development
items.answer: I think collective action problems are easier to resolve when people don't just believe they're collective action problems and can't be resolved. The first thing is, as someone building the technology, ask yourself not what do I think other people are going to do but what should I do. You have an increment of causal power, and if you think that the likely trajectory of your choices is going to lead to harm for a group of people or more widely, then you shouldn't do it. If people modeled that correctly, then we wouldn't have so much of a collective action problem because it would dissipate under the force of a higher level of moral motivation. Now in reality, we live in the world of non-ideal theory. There are people abstaining and making good decisions and setting good examples and setting precedents. That can slow the trajectory of a technology, which can also open up new avenues for containing risk and doing other things, which is very important.

items.question: How do you think governance may need to change as advanced technologies acquire more profound potential consequences?
items.object: Collective governance of advanced technologies
items.answer: The collective action problem probably also needs to be tackled head-on at some point. You see this in genetic research and things like that. There's certain things that you absolutely should not do. And then we also want to triple-lock it. So we make it illegal and we try and create international treaties and things like that. I can imagine that could one day be a necessary protocol for certain forms of AI or scientific research. I guess one deep question is: are advanced technologies by themselves laden with greater inherent risk? Should we for that reason expect to need stronger regulatory structures in the future than we have at present? That is hard to say, but it does seem like many of these new technologies have consequences latent within their potential that are quite profound. Nanotechnology certainly has that character, genetic modification. We may need to level up as a society and as a world community in terms of trying to take collective control of these forces that were previously maybe well directed through existing institutions and market mechanisms. I think it's a bit of an open question what AGI governance looks like.

Nanotechnology certainly has that character, genetic modification.

We may need to level up as a society and as a world community in terms of trying to take collective control of these forces that were previously maybe well directed through existing institutions and market mechanisms. I think it's a bit of an open question what AGI governance looks like, and fortunately other people are thinking a lot of time into thinking about.

The response suggests that the profound potential consequences of emerging technologies may require more collective societal control than existing institutions and market mechanisms provide.

items.question: How has your understanding of toleration shaped the direction you want your research to take?
items.object: Toleration as a guiding aim of his research
items.answer: The overall arc of my research is definitely in the direction of essentially more tolerant approaches where we live together and we try to unlock visions of the future where we're able to flourish together. The importance of toleration is not something that was always apparent to me when I was a younger philosopher. I definitely was more strident and I thought, well, just go for it, fight injustice, etc. But it seems to me that there's so much pluralism in the world and so much power that managing to strike an equilibrium where people are able to flourish on their own terms is a really valuable thing. And I think it could even be really important for some of the conversations about AI that I imagine will take place in the next five or ten years.

items.question: How do you think a community should handle disagreement about whether AI is conscious when no shared method can settle it?
items.object: Fundamental disagreement about AI consciousness
items.answer: One area in which there may be new fundamental disagreement is this question of AI consciousness. It may be that some people believe that AI has it. Some people may just avowedly disbelieve it. And there may be no empirical or philosophical method that we can bring to bear to solve this issue. So for me the question is, if we can't solve it at the level of first principle, how can we solve it as a community that still needs to live together? In that context I think that many of the things we've spoken about today are sensible. If there's a risk of extreme harm by doing one thing, then perhaps we can try and take that option off the table, and even those of us who are not worried about the concern can see that it has some standing. But more generally, I think that we're going to have to tolerate disagreement in this space.

items.question: What does democratic hope mean to you as an aim your work might support?
items.object: Democratic hope
items.answer: One thing I've been thinking about a lot lately is the character of what I would call democratic hope. When people have fundamental disagreements, they can decide: am I going to keep going and try to live with people in this community, or am I going to opt out? And that way leads to conflict and violence and things like that. I think that everyone has to have the requisite amount of hope to believe that their voice will be heard and that there's a way forward. Insofar as my work can help people believe in that and think, well, there's this way, or maybe if it doesn't work this way, we can find another pathway to this way of productively living together, then that's something that I would be very grateful for.
